extracted.intended_audience: pharmaceutical patent prosecutors, patent attorneys, and in-house counsel drafting pharma patents
extracted.subtask_description: Practical drafting guidance for preparing patent applications and claims for pharmaceutical inventions (APIs, salts, polymorphs, methods, formulations) with attention to claim strategies, support, and regulatory listing implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Claims - The Core Asset
rubrics_metrics.description: For a pharmaceutical, the composition-of-matter claim is the keystone. It typically claims a chemical compound or class of compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting choices include claiming the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) by structure, by name, by Markush group, or as a salt/polymorph. Composition claims are the primary defensive and exclusionary asset for a drug.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush Groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush claim recites a closed group of alternatives ("R1 is selected from the group consisting of methyl, ethyl, propyl"). Markush is the standard format for genus claims in chemistry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The group must be sufficiently disclosed to support written description; broad groups need representative species. Ensure adequate disclosure of representative members and avoid overbroad Markush lists without supporting examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Treatment Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming methods of treating disease (e.g., "A method of treating disease X comprising administering compound Y to a patient in need thereof").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File method-of-treatment claims in addition to composition claims because they reach pharmacy infringement and inducement liability against marketing. Use clear claim language (patient in need thereof, dosing/context) and include supporting data where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Manufacture Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Process claims that protect the synthesis route for a compound or formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly valuable when the route is novel and difficult to design around. Be aware process claims are subject to special infringement rules under 35 U.S.C. §271(g) for products imported into the U.S.; consider whether the process provides meaningful protection in your target markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polymorph and Crystal Form Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim novel crystalline/polymorphic forms (e.g., Form I, Form II) which can affect bioavailability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polymorphs can be claimed by powder XRD pattern, melting point, FTIR characteristic peaks. These claims can support Orange Book listings and are commonly implicated in Hatch-Waxman litigation. Provide analytical characterization data to define and support the claimed form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salt Forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Different pharmaceutically acceptable salts of the same active compound can be separately patentable if novel and non-obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salt selection patents are common follow-ons; demonstrate novelty/non-obviousness and provide supporting data (e.g., improved properties). Consider claiming salts explicitly and include examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dosing Regimen Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to specific dosing regimens, e.g., "administering compound Y at a dose of Z mg per day in a 28-day cycle."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dosing/regimen claims are often patented separately and can provide a second wave of protection after composition patents expire. Draft clearly defined regimen parameters (dose, schedule, duration) and support with pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic or clinical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination Therapy Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to administering two or more compounds together ("A method comprising administering compound A and compound B").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when the combination shows synergy or improved tolerability. Provide evidence of synergistic effect or unexpected benefits to strengthen non-obviousness and enablement arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus-to-Species Strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing strategy recommending an early genus application covering a broad class and later species applications as the lead emerges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File a genus application early; file species applications for the specific lead compound as it becomes defined. Coordinate foreign filing strategy carefully because of data exclusivity and considerations like supplementary protection certificates (SPC) and patent term extensions (PTE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Disparaging the Active
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid negative statements about other compounds in the specification (e.g., "compound X has poor bioavailability...").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements disparaging an active can be used against you in obviousness proceedings if you later seek to broaden coverage to that active. Maintain neutral language and avoid admissions that could support motivation to combine or obviousness arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive Data in the Spec
rubrics_metrics.description: Including in-vitro and in-vivo data in the specification to support enablement and inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples with measured potency, selectivity, half-life, toxicity, and other relevant pharmacological data. Such data supports enablement and can form the basis for arguments of unexpected results to overcome obviousness rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hatch-Waxman and Orange Book
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations for listing patents in the FDA's Orange Book and Hatch-Waxman litigation implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents covering an FDA-approved drug must be listed in the Orange Book; listed patents trigger the 30-month stay in Hatch-Waxman litigation. Listing decisions affect drafting choices: composition and formulation patents are listable; pure method-of-manufacture patents are not. Draft claims with awareness of whether they will be listable and the strategic consequences.
